cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is partitioned-edit consistency debt?
cards.answer: The residue left when a global change is executed as many independent local edits: each unit passes its own checks, but cross-unit invariants (type signatures, call contracts, shared schemas, naming conventions) are owned by no worker, so the aggregate lands locally valid but globally inconsistent.

cards.heading: Why it happens
cards.question: Why does partitioning a change into independent units create this debt, rather than it being a sign of sloppy work?
cards.answer: It is structural: partitioning is what makes parallel work cheap, because each worker sees only its own unit — and that same narrowness makes any invariant spanning two or more units invisible to every worker.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.question: In the reported case, a per-file type-tightening sweep hit a 100% fix rate on its lint backlog. What did it also produce?
cards.answer: 61 downstream type errors in files the sweep never touched, because a signature tightened in one file broke a contract in its callers.

cards.heading: Silent failure at the dashboard
cards.question: Why is a per-unit completion metric a bad signal for this kind of debt?
cards.answer: Per-unit success metrics stay green even when cross-unit invariants are broken, since only properties spanning two-plus units are affected — so a 'perfect' completion rate can coincide with exactly when the debt is largest.

cards.heading: Mitigations and their cost
cards.question: What do the three mitigations for partitioned-edit consistency debt have in common?
cards.answer: Each trades back some of the parallelism the partition bought: running a global check after the fan-out, partitioning along the invariant instead of the file, or reserving cross-boundary edit classes for a coordinating pass.
